claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: Across cytoarchitectonic areas, Te1.0 shows the highest myelination contrast.
claims.source: Across cytoarchitectonic areas, Te1.0 shows the highest myelination contrast.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claims.claim: The average tonotopic pattern highlights the Heschl's Gyrus as preferring low frequencies for the most part, while surrounding areas prefer high frequencies.
claims.source: The average tonotopic pattern highlights the Heschl's Gyrus as, for the most part, preferring low frequencies, while surrounding areas (in posterior antero-medial and antero-lateral directions) prefer high frequencies (see Figure 10).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: The high-frequency areas form an inverted 'V' pattern surrounding the Heschl's Gyrus.
claims.source: The high-frequency areas form an inverted 'V' pattern surrounding the Heschl's Gyrus (Da Costa et al., 2011; Moerel et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations.

claims.claim: Cytoarchitectonic primary cortical areas (Te1) cover the Heschl's Gyrus, with the core (Te1.0) in its middle section which at the group level appears characterized by mainly low-frequency preference.
claims.source: Cytoarchitectonic primary cortical areas (Te1) cover the Heschl's Gyrus, with the core (Te1.0) in its middle section which (at the group level) appears characterized by mainly low-frequency preference (see Figure 10).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: Area Te1.1, located medial to Te1.0, may reflect an intermediate processing stage between primary and belt areas and covers one tonotopic gradient going from high to low in an antero-medial to postero-lateral direction.
claims.source: Located medial to Te1.0, area Te1.1 may reflect an intermediate processing stage between primary and belt areas (Moerel et al., 2014) and covers one tonotopic gradient going from high to low in an antero-medial to postero-lateral direction.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claims.claim: Te2.2 covers a posterior portion of the tonotopic gradient running in the posterior to anterior direction.
claims.source: Te2.2 covers a posterior portion of the tonotopic gradient running in the posterior to anterior direction.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claims.claim: Te2.1, covering an intermediate location between Te2.2 and Te1.0/Te1.2, overlaps with a low-frequency preferring region in the lateral portion of the Heschl's sulcus.
claims.source: Te2.1, covering an intermediate location between Te2.2 and Te1.0/Te1.2, overlaps with a low-frequency preferring region in the lateral portion of the Heschl's sulcus.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data.

claims.claim: Te3 covers a low-frequency portion of the tonotopic maps along the superior temporal gyrus.
claims.source: Finally, Te3 covers a low-frequency portion of the tonotopic maps along the superior temporal gyrus (Moerel et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claims.claim: The superior temporal plane shows considerable macro-anatomical variability across individuals.
claims.source: The superior temporal plane shows considerable macro-anatomical variability across individuals (Pfeifer, 1921; Pfeifer, 1936; Von Economo and Horn, 1930; Rademacher et al., 1993; Zoellner et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claims.claim: Large inter-individual differences in the superior temporal plane are detrimental to functional and anatomical in vivo investigations of the temporal lobe if unaccounted for.
claims.source: If unaccounted for, these large inter-individual differences are detrimental to functional (and anatomical) in vivo investigations of the temporal lobe as they limit the efficacy of alignment procedures that are used in group studies.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a consequence of variability.

claims.claim: When signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is limited, investigators rely on averaging functional and anatomical information both within a subject and across subjects.
claims.source: In addition, when signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is limited, investigators rely on averaging functional (and anatomical) information, both within a subject (i.e. within a cortical area across voxels) and across subjects.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as current practice in the field.

claims.claim: Functional and anatomical localizers exist for some cortical regions in the temporal lobe (e.g., PAC, voice regions).
claims.source: While functional and anatomical localizers exist for some cortical regions in the temporal lobe (e.g., PAC -Moerel et al., 2012; voice regions - Belin et al., 2000), such localizers are not available for the majority of the auditory cortex.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claims.claim: Localizers are not available for the majority of the auditory cortex.
claims.source: While functional and anatomical localizers exist for some cortical regions in the temporal lobe (e.g., PAC -Moerel et al., 2012; voice regions - Belin et al., 2000), such localizers are not available for the majority of the auditory cortex.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation in the field.

claims.claim: Investigators often rely on available parcellations which result from postmortem or in vivo investigations in a population.
claims.source: As a consequence, investigators often rely on available parcellations (see, e.g., the procedure followed by Dick et al., 2012) which result from postmortem (or in vivo) investigations in a population and as a consequence rely on the quality of the inter-subject alignment.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claims.claim: The study used 10 individual brains available from the JuBrain cytoarchitectonic Atlas.
claims.source: We have used 10 individual brains available from the JuBrain cytoarchitectonic Atlas (The JuBrain atlas is available through the Atlas of the Human Brain Project https://jubrain.fz-juelich.de/ (Amunts and Zilles, 2015) together with a surface registration method that minimizes macro-anatomical variability around the transverse temporal gyrus (similar to Rosenke et al., 2018) to show that minimizing macro-anatomical variability in the superior temporal plane results in improved micro-anatomical correspondence across brains.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claims.claim: Minimizing macro-anatomical variability in the superior temporal plane results in improved micro-anatomical correspondence across brains.
claims.source: We have used 10 individual brains available from the JuBrain cytoarchitectonic Atlas (The JuBrain atlas is available through the Atlas of the Human Brain Project https://jubrain.fz-juelich.de/ (Amunts and Zilles, 2015) together with a surface registration method that minimizes macro-anatomical variability around the transverse temporal gyrus (similar to Rosenke et al., 2018) to show that minimizing macro-anatomical variability in the superior temporal plane results in improved micro-anatomical correspondence across brains.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a key finding of the study.

claims.claim: The study provides a more accurate probabilistic atlas of the cytoarchitectonic areas in the temporal lobe.
claims.source: Our results have two potential benefits for the auditory neuroscience community. First, by providing a more accurate (i.e. with improved inter subject alignment) probabilistic atlas of the cytoarchitectonic areas in the temporal lobe, we provide a valuable resource for those studies that rely on a parcellation scheme.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a contribution of the study.

claims.claim: Minimizing a particular set of macro-anatomical features results in a more accurate micro-anatomical alignment.
claims.source: Second, we show that minimizing a particular set of macro-anatomical features results in a more accurate micro-anatomical alignment, and thus that using local landmarks for aligning temporal regions results in a better alignment of cytoarchitectonic areas.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a key finding of the study.

claims.claim: Using local landmarks for aligning temporal regions results in a better alignment of cytoarchitectonic areas.
claims.source: Second, we show that minimizing a particular set of macro-anatomical features results in a more accurate micro-anatomical alignment, and thus that using local landmarks for aligning temporal regions results in a better alignment of cytoarchitectonic areas.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a key finding of the study.

claims.claim: The study justifies the use of local landmark approaches when aligning individual temporal cortices with each other or to a template.
claims.source: This justifies the use of these approaches (the one we propose here or others that have been proposed before Kang et al., 2004; Desai et al., 2005) when aligning individual temporal cortices with each other (or to a template).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion of the study.

claims.claim: Applying a surface registration for inter-subject alignment required accurate segmentation of the postmortem MRI dataset.
claims.source: Applying a surface registration for inter-subject alignment required accurate segmentation of the postmortem MRI dataset.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a methodological requirement.

claims.claim: The available 10 brains showed typical variations in the morphology of the Heschl's Gyrus, with a single Heschl's Gyrus being the most prevalent.
claims.source: The availabe 10 brains showed typical variations in the morphology of the Heschl's Gyrus (with a single Heschl's Gyrus being the most prevalent one), as well as cases in which the Heschl's Gyrus was continuous to the anterior portion of the superior temporal gyrus (Heschl, 1878).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation from the data.

claims.claim: Standard CBA minimizes macro-anatomical variation across subjects across the whole brain in a coarse to fine iterative approach.
claims.source: The standard approach minimizes macro-anatomical variation across subjects (i.e. maximizes the overlap of the curvature maps) across the whole brain (in a coarse to fine iterative approach).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a description of standard CBA.

claims.claim: Standard CBA is driven by the major anatomical landmarks including the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus.
claims.source: As such, standard CBA is driven by the major anatomical landmarks including the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a characteristic of standard CBA.

claims.claim: Standard CBA can result in compromised alignment of smaller but consistent anatomical features such as the Heschl's Gyrus.
claims.source: This, however, can result in compromised alignment of smaller (but consistent) anatomical features such as the Heschl's Gyrus.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of standard CBA.

claims.claim: The necessity to use local landmarks to guide the alignment of temporal regions has been considered in previous research.
claims.source: For this reason, here we have considered the application of an approach tailored to the superior temporal plane. The necessity to use local landmarks to guide the alignment of temporal regions has been considered in previous research (Kang et al., 2004; Desai et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claims.claim: Previous approaches defined macro-anatomical points or lines covering the main gyri and sulci in the temporal cortex for alignment.
claims.source: By defining macro-anatomical points in the temporal cortex (Kang et al., 2004) or lines covering the main gyri and sulci (Desai et al., 2005) both linear and non-linear alignment procedures have been compared to global spherical alignment and volumetric approaches.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claims.claim: The study provided additional landmarks (the Heschl's Gyrus, the superior temporal gyrus/sulcus and middle temporal gyrus) to the CBA procedure.
claims.source: Here, we provided additional landmarks (the Heschl's Gyrus, the superior temporal gyrus/sulcus and middle temporal gyrus) to the CBA procedure and, differently from previous approaches (that considered only the local landmarks when aligning the temporal cortex), we optimized alignment of both local and global macro-anatomical features.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as the approach taken in the study.

claims.claim: The study optimized alignment of both local and global macro-anatomical features, differently from previous approaches that considered only local landmarks.
claims.source: Here, we provided additional landmarks (the Heschl's Gyrus, the superior temporal gyrus/sulcus and middle temporal gyrus) to the CBA procedure and, differently from previous approaches (that considered only the local landmarks when aligning the temporal cortex), we optimized alignment of both local and global macro-anatomical features.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a distinction from previous approaches.

claims.claim: CBA+ improved the alignment across subjects in the superior temporal cortex compared to standard CBA.
claims.source: By doing so, we improved the alignment across subjects in the superior temporal cortex (see e.g. the difference in the average curvature maps between standard CBA and CBA+ in Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Both CBA and CBA+ greatly improved the macro-anatomical correspondence when compared to a rigid body procedure.
claims.source: Both the CBA and CBA+ approach greatly improved the macro-anatomical correspondence when compared to a rigid body procedure (which by sampling the volumetric data on surfaces already offers an improvement compared to the original volumetric alignment - see Figure 8 and Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claims.claim: The result of improved macro-anatomical correspondence with CBA and CBA+ is in line with previously reported increased macro-anatomical correspondence obtained when using alignment procedures that use local landmarks.
claims.source: This result is in line with the previously reported increased macro-anatomical correspondence obtained when using alignment procedures that use local landmarks (Kang et al., 2004; Desai et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claims.claim: The advantage of the tailored approach (CBA+) is stronger in the right hemisphere, with some residual misalignment for the left Heschl's Gyrus.
claims.source: The advantage of the tailored approach (CBA+, rightmost column in Figure 1) is stronger in the right hemisphere, with some residual misalignment for the left Heschl's Gyrus.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The difference in performance between hemispheres could be explained by the larger prevalence in the left hemisphere of cases with the Heschl's Gyrus merging with the anterior portion of the superior temporal gyrus (split superior temporal gyrus cases).
claims.source: This difference in performance could be explained by the larger prevalence (within our sample) in the left hemisphere of cases with the Heschl's Gyrus merging with the anterior portion of the superior temporal gyrus (i.e. split superior temporal gyrus cases; two in the left and one in the right hemisphere).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a possible explanation.

claims.claim: A larger sample could allow evaluating the impact of the split superior temporal gyrus variation on alignment by evaluating alignment separately with and without such cases.
claims.source: In the future, a larger sample could allow evaluating this issue, as well as the impact that the inclusion of this macro-anatomical variation has on the alignment of regions close to the superior temporal gyrus, by evaluating the alignment separately (with and without) such cases.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion for future research.

claims.claim: Tailoring the alignment of the temporal lobe to local landmarks is motivated by the expectation that minimizing macro-anatomy will result in improved micro-anatomical alignment.
claims.source: Tailoring the alignment of the temporal lobe to local landmarks is motivated by the expectation that minimizing macro-anatomy will consequently result in improved micro-anatomical alignment (i.e. the alignment of cortical areas in the temporal lobe) and that this in turn improves functional alignment (assuming that function and micro-anatomy co-localize).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as the motivation for the approach.

claims.claim: Previous studies have shown that approaches that use local landmarks result in improved group functional activation.
claims.source: While previous studies have shown that approaches that use local landmarks result in improved group functional activation (Kang et al., 2004; Desai et al., 2005), here we addressed the much required validation of how well such an approach reduces the underlying micro-anatomical variability.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claims.claim: Improving macro-anatomical correspondence resulted in improved overlap of the cytoarchitectonic areas across subjects.
claims.source: Improving macro-anatomical correspondence resulted in improved overlap of the cytoarchitectonic areas across subjects.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a key finding.

claims.claim: As a result of CBA+ alignment, the micro-anatomically defined areas were smaller and the probability for a vertex to be labeled as belonging to the same area across the postmortem samples was higher.
claims.source: As a result of the CBA+ alignment, the micro-anatomically defined areas were smaller and the probability for a vertex to be labeled as belonging to the same area across the postmortem samples was higher (see Figures 2–7 and the histograms in Figure 8 and Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figures 2-9.

claims.claim: The tailored approach (CBA+) resulted in increased overlap in all areas but especially in those on Heschl's Gyrus or immediately adjacent to it (Te1.0, Te1.1, Te1.2 and Te2.1).
claims.source: The tailored approach (CBA+) resulted in increased overlap (also compared to standard CBA) in all areas but especially in those on Heschl's Gyrus or immediately adjacent to it (Te1.0, Te1.1, Te1.2 and Te2.1 - see Table 1 and Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claims.claim: The increased overlap in areas on or adjacent to Heschl's Gyrus is a direct consequence of defining the most anterior Heschl's Gyrus as an additional landmark for alignment.
claims.source: This result is a direct consequence of defining the (most anterior) Heschl's Gyrus as an additional landmark for alignment.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an explanation for the result.

claims.claim: The most anterior Heschl's Gyrus was recognized as the putative location of primary auditory cortex in the case of a complete duplication on the basis of myelo-architecture.
claims.source: The most anterior Heschl's Gyrus was recognized as the putative location of primary auditory cortex in the case of a complete duplication on the basis of myelo-architecture (Hackett et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claims.claim: When the most anterior Heschl's Gyrus is not used as a landmark, the duplication of the Heschl's Gyrus results in poorer matching across subjects.
claims.source: When this anatomical landmark is not used, the duplication of the Heschl's Gyrus results in poorer matching across subjects (i.e. the most posterior duplication of some subjects is aligned to the single Heschl's Gyrus of other subjects).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an explanation for the importance of the landmark.

claims.claim: The postmortem dataset includes six Heschl's Gyrus duplication cases (four in the right and two in the left hemisphere).
claims.source: The postmortem dataset includes six Heschl's Gyrus duplication cases (four in the right and two in the left hemisphere).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a characteristic of the dataset.

claims.claim: Follow-up studies are needed to evaluate the effect of an incomplete duplication of Heschl's Gyrus.
claims.source: Follow-up studies are needed to evaluate the effect of an incomplete duplication of Heschl's Gyrus.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion for future research.

claims.claim: Previous myelo-architecture studies reported a shift of primary areas toward the intermediate Heschl's sulcus in the case of an incomplete duplication.
claims.source: As previous myelo-architecture studies reported a shift of primary areas toward the intermediate Heschl's sulcus in the case of an incomplete duplication (Hackett et al., 2001), a partial alignment of the primary areas (Te1.0 and Te1.1) may be expected.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claims.claim: Examining the effect of an incomplete duplication on micro-anatomical alignment may provide additional insights for further refinement of the alignment procedure.
claims.source: Examining the effect of an incomplete duplication on micro-anatomical alignment may provide additional insights for a further refinement of the alignment procedure we propose here.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion for future research.

claims.claim: Areas along the superior temporal gyrus/sulcus and middle temporal gyrus landmarks were also better realigned by CBA+, though to a lesser degree than areas on Heschl's Gyrus.
claims.source: In addition to the anterior Heschl's Gyrus, CBA+ includes the superior temporal gyrus/sulcus and middle temporal gyrus as anatomical landmarks. While to a lesser degree than the areas on Heschl's Gyrus, areas along these landmarks were also better realigned by CBA+.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation from the data.

claims.claim: Favoring the superior temporal gyrus/sulcus and middle temporal gyrus with respect to other major landmarks on the cortex is beneficial for the alignment of temporal areas.
claims.source: This indicates that favoring these gyri/sulci with respect to other major landmarks on the cortex is beneficial for the alignment of temporal areas.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the results.

claims.claim: The improved cytoarchitectonic overlap obtained with CBA+ suggests that this approach may be relevant for the functional and anatomical investigation of auditory temporal areas in vivo.
claims.source: The improved cytoarchitectonic overlap obtained with CBA+ suggests that this approach may be relevant for the functional and anatomical investigation of (auditory) temporal areas in vivo, as well as the investigation (postmortem and in vivo ) of other cortical regions in which macro-anatomical variability is high.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion and suggestion.

claims.claim: The study makes the individual hemisphere surface models and the individual cytoarchitectonic areas publicly available.
claims.source: We make the individual hemisphere surface models and the individual cytoarchitectonic areas used in this study publicly available at https://kg.ebrains.eu/search/instances/Dataset/ff71a4d1-ea14-4ed6-898e-b92d95b3c446.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a contribution of the study.

claims.claim: The publicly available dataset could be used to compare the performance of different landmark based approaches and non-linear volumetric approaches to CBA+.
claims.source: In follow-up investigations, this publicly available data set could also be used to compare the performance of different landmark based approaches that use only local landmarks (Kang et al., 2004; Desai et al., 2005) as well as non-linear volumetric approaches to CBA+.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion for future research.

claims.claim: The study applied CBA+ to align anatomical and functional data collected at 7 Tesla across individuals.
claims.source: To showcase the application of CBA+ to the analysis of in vivo MRI data, we applied the same procedure to align anatomical and functional data collected at 7 Tesla across individuals.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an application of the method.

claims.claim: The pattern of myelin related intra cortical contrast followed previous reports.
claims.source: The pattern of myelin related intra cortical contrast followed previous reports (Glasser and Van Essen, 2011; Dick et al., 2012; De Martino et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claims.claim: The alignment to the cytoarchitectonic atlas shows a high myelin-related contrast in area Te1.0, in agreement with previous studies.
claims.source: The alignment to the cytoarchitectonic atlas shows a high myelin-related contrast in area Te1.0, in agreement with previous studies (Dick et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claims.claim: A more clear cut separation between Te1.0 and Te1.1 may require the evaluation of myelin-related contrast across depths.
claims.source: While subtle differences between Te1.0 and Te1.1 were already noticeable, a more clear cut separation between these regions may require the evaluation of myelin-related contrast across depths similarly to previous approaches (Dick et al., 2012; De Martino et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion for future research.

claims.claim: Future investigations may evaluate the information provided by intra anatomical contrast resulting from in vivo MRI acquisitions other than the one considered in the study.
claims.source: In addition, future investigations may evaluate the information provided by intra anatomical contrast resulting from in vivo MRI acquisitions other than the one we considered here (e.g. using the orientation of intra-cortical fibers [McNab et al., 2013; Gulban et al., 2018a]).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion for future research.

claims.claim: The group tonotopy maps derived from the in vivo data follow previous reports.
claims.source: The group tonotopy maps we derived from the in vivo data follow previous reports (Dick et al., 2012; Moerel et al., 2014; Besle et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claims.claim: The group tonotopy maps show one gradient within area Te1.1 progressing from high to low frequencies in antero-medial to postero-lateral direction.
claims.source: In particular, they show one gradient within area Te1.1 progressing from high to low frequencies in antero-medial to postero-lateral direction.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation from the data.

claims.claim: Based on the average maps, a full tonotopic gradient was not visible in Te1.0, which was corresponding mainly with the low frequency area on medial Heschl's Gyrus.
claims.source: Based on the average maps, a full tonotopic gradient was not visible in Te1.0, which was corresponding mainly with the low frequency area on medial Heschl's Gyrus.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation from the data.

claims.claim: The pattern in Te1.0 may be the result of excessive smoothing caused by inter-subject averaging that highlights the larger frequency gradient progressing in the anterior-posterior direction on the planum temporale.
claims.source: This pattern may be the result of excessive smoothing caused by inter-subject averaging that highlights the larger frequency gradient that in tonotopic maps progresses in the anterior-posterior direction on the planum temporale and thus favors the interpretation of the pattern within larger cortical areas (Moerel et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a possible explanation.

claims.claim: Future studies are needed to quantify the information that can be leveraged from individual in vivo MRI data for characterizing the cytoarchitectonic areas.
claims.source: While future studies are needed to quantify the information that can be leveraged from individual in vivo MRI data for characterizing the cytoarchitectonic areas, our preliminary results indicate that individual tonotopic [and myelin] maps (supplement figures to Figure 10) provide more fine grained information (within smaller areas such as e.g. Te1.0) (Moerel et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a suggestion for future research.

claims.claim: Individual tonotopic and myelin maps provide more fine grained information within smaller areas such as Te1.0.
claims.source: While future studies are needed to quantify the information that can be leveraged from individual in vivo MRI data for characterizing the cytoarchitectonic areas, our preliminary results indicate that individual tonotopic [and myelin] maps (supplement figures to Figure 10) provide more fine grained information (within smaller areas such as e.g. Te1.0) (Moerel et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figure 10 supplements.

claims.claim: Te2.2 captured the most posterior portion of the larger tonotopic gradient that runs in a direction orthogonal to Heschl's Gyrus.
claims.source: Te2.2 captured the most posterior portion of the larger tonotopic gradient that, consistently with previous reports, we identify as running in a direction orthogonal to Heschl's Gyrus (Moerel et al., 2014; Besle et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claims.claim: Te2.1 and Te3 covered low-frequency preferring regions of the tonotopic map in the lateral portion of the Heschl's sulcus and the superior temporal gyrus.
claims.source: The other cytoarchitectonic regions that overlapped with our functional acquisition field of view (Te2.1 and Te3) covered low-frequency preferring regions of the tonotopic map in the lateral portion of the Heschl's sulcus and the superior temporal gyrus.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation from the data.

claims.claim: The results argue for the necessity of interpreting large-scale tonotopic maps, which by themselves do not allow defining the borders between superior temporal cortical areas.
claims.source: These results argue for the necessity of interpreting large-scale tonotopic maps, which by themselves do not allow defining the borders between superior temporal cortical areas (Moerel et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation.

claims.claim: A large tonotopic gradient runs in a posterior to anterior direction.
claims.source: A large tonotopic gradient unarguably runs in a posterior to anterior direction Da Costa et al., 2011; Besle et al., 2018.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claims.claim: Equating the large posterior to anterior tonotopic gradient with the gradient that identifies the primary auditory cortex results in a view in which the core lies orthogonal to Heschl's Gyrus.
claims.source: Equating this gradient with the gradient that identifies the primary auditory cortex results in a view in which the core lies orthogonal to Heschl's Gyrus (Da Costa et al., 2011; Saenz and Langers, 2014; Besle et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claims.claim: The cytoarchitectonic areas, now restricted in size by better aligning macro-anatomy, suggest that the auditory core (Te1) runs along Heschl's Gyrus (the 'classical' view).
claims.source: On the other hand, the cytoarchitectonic areas -now restricted in size by better aligning macro-anatomy- suggest that the auditory core (Te1) runs along Heschl's Gyrus (i.e. the 'classical' view; Dick et al., 2012; Moerel et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations.

claims.claim: The view that the auditory core runs along Heschl's Gyrus is strengthened by the combined interpretation of myelin and tonotopy as well as other auditory cortical functional characteristics.
claims.source: This view is strengthened by the combined interpretation of myelin and tonotopy (see Figure 10 and results in Dick et al., 2012; Moerel et al., 2014) as well as other auditory cortical functional characteristics (e.g. frequency selectivity; Moerel et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations and shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: Interesting differences exist between the surface projection of the cytoarchitectonic areas compared to a recent parcellation of the temporal lobe derived solely from in vivo imaging (Glasser et al., 2016).
claims.source: Interesting differences exist between the surface projection of the cytoarchitectonic areas compared to a recent parcellation of the temporal lobe derived solely from in vivo imaging (Glasser et al., 2016 - see Figure 11).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation and shown in Figure 11.

claims.claim: Cytoarchitectonic areas Te1.1, Te1.0 and Te1.2 lie postero-medial to antero-lateral along the Heschl's Gyrus.
claims.source: Cytoarchitectonic areas Te1.1, Te1.0 and Te1.2 lie postero-medial to antero-lateral along the Heschl's Gyrus.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a description of the cytoarchitectonic areas.

claims.claim: The most lateral subdivision (Te1.2) has been suggested to be the human homologue of area RT in the monkey (part of the auditory core) or part of the lateral belt.
claims.source: The most lateral subdivision (Te1.2) has been suggested to be the human homologue of area RT in the monkey (and thus part of the auditory core) or part of the lateral belt (Moerel et al., 2014).

results.result: CBA+, a novel cortical surface registration method incorporating anatomical priors (anterior Heschl's Gyrus, superior temporal gyrus, superior temporal sulcus, and middle temporal gyrus), was developed and validated using cytoarchitectonic areas from 10 postmortem brains. CBA+ demonstrated superior performance compared to volumetric alignment, rigid body alignment, and standard curvature-based alignment (CBA) in aligning cytoarchitectonic areas of the auditory cortex, with improved macro-anatomical alignment resulting in improved micro-anatomical correspondence.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C6, C27-C33, C40-C43, C84-C88, and C149 collectively establish that CBA+ was developed, validated on 10 brains using cytoarchitectonic areas, and demonstrated superior alignment compared to other methods. The validation is supported by quantitative metrics (Dice coefficients in Tables 1-2, histograms in Figures 8-9) and visual evidence (Figures 1-7, 45-47) showing improved overlap of cytoarchitectonic areas. The claim that improved macro-anatomical alignment leads to improved micro-anatomical correspondence (C6, C84) is directly demonstrated by the data.

results.result: CBA and CBA+ both improved macro-anatomical alignment in the temporal lobe compared to rigid body alignment, as evidenced by increased sharpness of average curvature maps and improved definition of the average folded mesh. CBA+ showed particular improvement over standard CBA in the right hemisphere at the level of Heschl's Gyrus, though some residual misalignment remained in the left hemisphere.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47, C53, C99-C100, and C102 are supported by visual evidence in Figure 1 showing sharper average curvature maps and more prominently defined Heschl's Gyrus with CBA+. The hemispheric differences (C102) are documented and shown in the figures. The claims are based on qualitative visual assessment which is appropriate for evaluating macro-anatomical alignment quality.

results.result: CBA+ improved the overlap of all cytoarchitectonic areas across the 10 brains, with the largest improvements observed for areas along Heschl's Gyrus (Te1.0, Te1.1, Te1.2) and Te2.1. For areas in the planum temporale (Te2.1, Te2.2) and superior temporal gyrus/sulcus (Te3, STS1, STS2), all surface approaches improved alignment compared to volumetric alignment, with CBA+ providing additional benefit especially for Te2.1.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59, C107-C109 are supported by quantitative data in Tables 1-2 (Dice coefficients), Figures 8-9 (histograms), and Figures 2-7 (probabilistic overlap maps). The differential effects across regions are documented with specific metrics. The leave-one-out validation approach (C43) provides robust evidence for the improved overlap claims.

results.result: The postmortem sample exhibited typical morphological variations in Heschl's Gyrus, including variation in the number of Heschl's Gyri (1, 1.5, or 2) and rare cases of split superior temporal gyrus (3 hemispheres: 1 right, 2 left). The split superior temporal gyrus pattern, first described by Heschl in 1878, occurred in approximately 10% of brains and was approximately eight times more likely in the left hemisphere.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52, C91, and C113 document anatomical variations observed in the dataset with specific counts and are supported by Figure 13. The historical context (C51-C52) is appropriately cited to Heschl, 1878 and Rademacher et al., 1993. These are descriptive observations of the sample characteristics.

results.result: In split superior temporal gyrus cases, the gyrus was defined as continuous (bridging the intermediate sulcus), which did not compromise alignment of the anterior Heschl's Gyrus. However, the larger prevalence of split cases in the left hemisphere may explain the stronger performance of CBA+ in the right hemisphere, and a larger sample would be needed to evaluate the impact of this variation on alignment.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 and C103-C104 describe a methodological decision and its potential impact. While C54 is a clear methodological statement, C55 claims no compromise to alignment but acknowledges uncertainty about effects on nearby regions. C103 offers a speculative explanation for hemispheric differences, and C104 explicitly calls for future work. The uncertainty about the full impact of this methodological choice on alignment quality is acknowledged by the authors.

results.result: CBA+ was applied to align in vivo 7T MRI data (anatomical and functional) across individuals and to the postmortem cytoarchitectonic atlas. This alignment enabled the projection of functional (tonotopic maps from natural sound encoding) and anatomical (myelin-related contrast from T1w/T2*w) information onto cytoarchitectonic areas and comparison with the Glasser et al. 2016 parcellation.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C34-C35, C44, C60-C65, and C122 describe the application of CBA+ to in vivo data and are supported by the methods description and Figure 10 showing the aligned data. The alignment procedure is clearly documented, and the resulting projections are visualized. This demonstrates the practical application of the method.

results.result: Myelin-related intra-cortical contrast from in vivo 7T data highlighted the medial Heschl's Gyrus as the most myelinated region in the temporal cortex, with Te1.0 showing the highest myelination contrast across cytoarchitectonic areas. This pattern followed previous reports.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 and C123-C124 are supported by Figure 10 showing myelin maps and are consistent with cited prior work (Glasser and Van Essen, 2011; Dick et al., 2012; De Martino et al., 2015). The observations are clearly visible in the presented data and align with established knowledge about primary auditory cortex myelination.

results.result: Group-level tonotopic maps from in vivo 7T fMRI showed that Heschl's Gyrus predominantly prefers low frequencies, while surrounding areas prefer high frequencies forming an inverted 'V' pattern. Cytoarchitectonic areas Te1 (including Te1.0, Te1.1, Te1.2) covered Heschl's Gyrus with specific tonotopic gradients, Te2.1 and Te2.2 covered portions of the planum temporale gradient, and Te3 covered low-frequency regions along the superior temporal gyrus.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C75, C127-C129, C133-C134 describe tonotopic patterns observed in the aligned in vivo data and are supported by Figure 10 and individual subject maps in supplementary figures. The patterns are consistent with cited prior work (Da Costa et al., 2011; Moerel et al., 2014; Besle et al., 2018). The correspondence between cytoarchitectonic areas and tonotopic features is clearly documented.

results.result: The absence of a full tonotopic gradient in Te1.0 at the group level may result from excessive smoothing during inter-subject averaging, which highlights larger gradients. Individual tonotopic and myelin maps provide more fine-grained information within smaller areas like Te1.0, though future studies are needed to quantify this.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C132 offer a speculative explanation (C130) for an observation (C129) and suggest that individual maps provide more detail (C132, supported by supplementary figures). However, C131 explicitly states that future studies are needed to quantify the information from individual data. The interpretation is plausible but requires additional validation.

results.result: Comparison between the cytoarchitectonic atlas and the Glasser et al. 2016 in vivo multi-modal parcellation revealed interesting differences in the superior temporal plane. The cytoarchitectonic areas Te1.1, Te1.0, and Te1.2 run along Heschl's Gyrus, while the Glasser parcellation divides Heschl's Gyrus into A1 (medial two-thirds) and medial belt (lateral portion). Additional differences exist in the planum temporale and superior temporal sulcus regions. These differences may reflect insufficient information in the in vivo data used for parcellation.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C148 describe observed differences between two atlases as shown in Figure 11. The differences are clearly documented and visualized. C148 offers a speculative explanation for the differences, which is appropriately qualified as a possibility. The comparison is descriptive and the differences are evident in the presented data.

results.result: The study used cytoarchitectonically labeled temporal cortical areas (Te1.0, Te1.1, Te1.2, Te2.1, Te2.2, Te3, STS1, STS2) and postmortem MR images from 10 brains from the JuBrain atlas. White matter-gray matter boundaries were segmented using a combination of image filtering techniques and histogram-based segmentation, which reduced manual correction requirements.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39 and C89 describe the data sources and preprocessing methods. The data source is clearly cited (JuBrain atlas, Morosan et al. 2001, etc.), and the segmentation approach is described with reference to Gulban et al., 2018b. The methods are documented in sufficient detail in the Materials and Methods section and Figure 12 shows the segmentation enhancement.

results.result: Standard CBA minimizes macro-anatomical variation across the whole brain in a coarse-to-fine iterative approach, driven by major anatomical landmarks including the superior temporal gyrus and sulcus. However, this can result in compromised alignment of smaller but consistent features like Heschl's Gyrus. Previous research has used local landmark approaches for temporal cortex alignment. The current study provided additional landmarks (Heschl's Gyrus, superior temporal gyrus/sulcus, middle temporal gyrus) to CBA and optimized alignment of both local and global macro-anatomical features.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C98 describe the rationale for CBA+ by contrasting it with standard CBA and previous approaches. C92-C94 describe standard CBA characteristics (supported by general knowledge and citations). C95-C96 cite previous work (Kang et al., 2004; Desai et al., 2005). C97-C98 describe the novel aspects of CBA+ as documented in the methods. The logical progression from problem to solution is well-supported.

results.result: The motivation for using local landmarks in temporal lobe alignment is the expectation that minimizing macro-anatomical differences will improve micro-anatomical and functional alignment. While previous studies showed improved group functional activation with local landmarks, this study validated the approach by demonstrating reduced micro-anatomical variability. The improved overlap in areas on or adjacent to Heschl's Gyrus results directly from using the anterior Heschl's Gyrus as a landmark, which is recognized as the putative location of primary auditory cortex in cases of complete duplication.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C106 and C110-C112 explain the rationale and mechanism for CBA+ improvements. C105 states the underlying assumption (supported by the study's results). C106 cites previous work showing functional improvements. C110-C112 explain why the anterior Heschl's Gyrus landmark is important, with C111 citing Hackett et al., 2001. The reasoning is logical and supported by the demonstrated improvements in overlap.

results.result: The human superior temporal plane displays high inter-individual macro-anatomical variation, with Heschl's Gyrus varying substantially in shape across individuals and hemispheres. This variation, along with reported shifts in primary auditory cortex location with morphological variation, raises questions about whether curvature-based alignment improves correspondence of micro-anatomically defined auditory areas. If unaccounted for, these differences are detrimental to functional and anatomical in vivo investigations.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C24-C26, C76-C77 establish the motivation for the study by citing well-documented anatomical variability (supported by multiple citations: Heschl, 1878; Rademacher et al., 1993; Hackett et al., 2001; Marie et al., 2015; Pfeifer, 1921; Von Economo and Horn, 1930; Zoellner et al., 2019). The logical inference that this variability questions the validity of standard alignment methods (C2, C26) is reasonable and motivates the study.

results.result: Multiple aspects of the study require follow-up investigation, including: the effect of incomplete Heschl's Gyrus duplication on alignment; evaluation of myelin-related contrast across cortical depths to better separate Te1.0 and Te1.1; assessment of other in vivo MRI contrasts (e.g., fiber orientation); quantification of information from individual in vivo data for characterizing cytoarchitectonic areas; comparison with other alignment approaches; and evaluation of CBA+ accuracy across all known macro-anatomical variations of Heschl's Gyrus.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C116, C121, C125-C126, C131, and C156 explicitly identify limitations and suggest future work. These are appropriately qualified as speculative (SPECULATION evidence type) and represent reasonable extensions of the current work. The authors appropriately acknowledge the boundaries of their current findings.

results.result: The results argue for careful interpretation of large-scale tonotopic maps, which alone do not define borders between superior temporal cortical areas. While a large tonotopic gradient runs posterior to anterior (which some equate with primary auditory cortex, placing the core orthogonal to Heschl's Gyrus), the cytoarchitectonic areas suggest the auditory core (Te1) runs along Heschl's Gyrus (the 'classical' view). This view is strengthened by combined interpretation of myelin, tonotopy, and other functional characteristics.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C139 present an interpretation of the results in the context of an ongoing debate about auditory cortex organization. C136-C137 cite one view (Da Costa et al., 2011; Saenz and Langers, 2014; Besle et al., 2018), while C138-C139 present the alternative view supported by the current data and cite supporting work (Dick et al., 2012; Moerel et al., 2014). The interpretation is supported by the combined evidence from multiple modalities shown in Figure 10.

results.result: The study's results have broad implications: reducing macro-anatomical variability and improving cytoarchitectural correspondence may reduce inter-subject variability of in vivo characteristics, resulting in more accurate definition of cortical areas. The results justify using landmark-based alignment for the temporal cortex and benefit studies relying on inter-individual alignment for statistical analysis. The improved cytoarchitectonic atlas serves as a resource for studies using cytoarchitectonically-defined ROIs. The approach is extendable to other cortical areas with high macro-anatomical variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C155 present the broader implications and contributions of the work. C150-C151 are logical inferences from the demonstrated improvements. C152 cites supporting prior work (Kang et al., 2004; Desai et al., 2005). C153-C154 describe concrete contributions (the atlas and validation of the approach). C155 is a reasonable speculation about extensibility. These claims appropriately summarize the significance of the findings.
